How to use this primer

This booklet teaches heat and mass transfer from zero, in the order the exam needs it. Read it once before the Complete Solutions. Each section has a green core idea box (learn this first), the key terms, the formulas with every symbol and unit, and a short worked example. Section 2 is a maths and units refresher: most marks lost in this course come from a wrong property table, a wrong length (D or r, height or A/p), or °C used where K is needed.

The pass set (from the Question Map): Section A topics A1 (modes and the conduction equation), A2 (walls, pipes, resistances), A3 (critical radius), A4 (fins) and A6 (boiling and condensation); Section B topics B1 (convection basics), B3 (flat-plate numericals), B5 (tube banks), B6 (natural convection) and B7 (mass transfer). Those topics are enough to write three full questions in each section.

The whole course on one page

Read the map from top to bottom: heat moves by conduction (through solids), convection (to a moving fluid) and radiation. Conduction problems are steady (walls, pipes, fins, insulation) or transient (bodies heating up or cooling). Convection problems are forced (plates, pipes, tube banks) or natural (buoyancy). Boiling and condensation are convection with phase change. Mass transfer is the same mathematics with concentration instead of temperature.

Maths, physics and units refresher

Almost every numerical follows one pattern: draw the picture → pick the right formula/correlation → get properties at the right temperature → substitute in SI units → check the answer is sensible.

Units you must convert without thinking

QuantityConversions
Length, area1 cm = 0.01 m, 1 mm = 0.001 m; 1 cm2 = 10−4 m2; 1 cm3 = 10−6 m3 (so 50 W/cm3 = 5×107 W/m3)
TemperatureT(K) = t(°C) + 273.15. Use K in radiation (T4), in β = 1/Tf and in C = P/RuT. A temperature difference is the same in K and °C.
Power, energy1 W = 1 J/s; 1 kW = 1000 W; 1 kJ = 1000 J; hfg in kJ/kg must be ×1000 in J/kg inside correlations
Pressure1 atm = 101.325 kPa; 1 kN/m2 = 1 kPa
Velocity15 m/min = 0.25 m/s
Diffusivity1 cm2/s = 10−4 m2/s

Logs, exponentials and roots

  • ln(a/b) = ln a − ln b; e−x for x small ≈ 1 − x. Cooling laws: θ/θi = e−bt; to find t: t = −ln(θ/θi)/b.
  • Quarter powers: x1/4 = √(√x). Example 108 → 100 (108 = (102)4).
  • Hyperbolic functions: sinh x = (ex − e−x)/2, cosh x = (ex + e−x)/2, tanh x = sinh x/cosh x; tanh 1 = 0.762, tanh 2 = 0.964, tanh 3 = 0.995.
  • Error function erf(η): read from a table; erf(0) = 0, erf(0.37) = 0.40, erf(0.5) = 0.52, erf(1) = 0.84, erf(2) = 0.995.
  • Log mean temperature difference: ΔTlm = (ΔT1 − ΔT2)/ln(ΔT1/ΔT2); always between the two differences.

Calculus you need

  • d/dx(xn) = nxn−1; ∫xndx = xn+1/(n + 1); ∫dx/x = ln x.
  • Equation d2θ/dx2 = m2θ has the solution θ = C1emx + C2e−mx (fins).
  • Equation d2T/dx2 = 0 gives T = C1x + C2 (plane wall); (1/r)d/dr(r dT/dr) = 0 gives T = C1ln r + C2 (pipe).
  • Average of a function over 0 to L: f̄ = (1/L)∫0Lf dx. If f ∝ x−1/2, f̄ = 2f(L).

Reading the property tables

  1. Decide the temperature: film Tf = (Ts + T∞)/2 for external flow and natural convection; bulk mean (Ti + Te)/2 for pipes and tube banks; liquid film at (Tsat + Ts)/2 for condensation.
  2. Read k, ν (or μ and ρ), Pr, cp from the air or water table (Cengel A-15, A-9), interpolating linearly: y = y1 + (x − x1)(y2 − y1)/(x2 − x1).
  3. Gas at a pressure other than 1 atm: k, μ, cp, Pr unchanged; ρ ∝ P, so ν ∝ 1/P.
  4. For saturated water (boiling, condensation) use the saturation table: Tsat, hfg, ρv.

Conduction and the conduction equation (A1)

Conduction is heat passing through a material from hot to cold by molecular collisions and free electrons. Fourier’s law Q = −kA dT/dx: the heat rate is proportional to the area and the temperature gradient. The conduction equation is energy conservation for a tiny element: heat in − heat out + heat generated = heat stored.

∂2T/∂x2 + ∂2T/∂y2 + ∂2T/∂z2 + ėgen/k = (1/α)∂T/∂t

SymbolMeaningUnit
Qheat transfer rateW
qheat flux Q/AW/m2
kthermal conductivityW/m K
Aarea normal to heat flowm2
αthermal diffusivity k/ρcpm2/s
ėgenheat generated per unit volumeW/m3
ρ, cpdensity, specific heatkg/m3, J/kg K
ttimes

Example: a 0.2 m wall (k = 1.2) with faces at 120 and 50 °C, area 15 m2: Q = 1.2 × 15 × 70/0.2 = 6300 W.

Thermal resistance networks (A2)

For steady one-dimensional heat flow, every layer behaves like an electrical resistor: Q = ΔT/R. Resistances in series add. Convection at a surface is also a resistance 1/(hA). So a wall with air on both sides is three resistors in a row.

ElementResistance R (K/W)
Plane wallL/(kA)
Convection film1/(hA)
Cylindrical layerln(r2/r1)/(2πkL)
Spherical shell(r2 − r1)/(4πkr1r2)
OverallUA = 1/ΣR
SymbolMeaningUnit
Rthermal resistanceK/W
hheat transfer coefficientW/m2K
Uoverall heat transfer coefficientW/m2K
r1, r2inner, outer radiusm
Lthickness (wall) or length (pipe)m

Example: steam pipe with glass wool: Rinside 0.106 + Rpipe 0.0002 + Rinsulation 2.348 + Routside 0.154 = 2.608 K/W; Q = 315/2.608 = 121 W per metre. The insulation does almost all the work.

Critical radius of insulation (A3)

Adding insulation to a thin pipe adds conduction resistance but also enlarges the outer surface, which lowers the convection resistance. Total resistance is lowest (heat loss highest) at the critical radius rcr = k/h for a cylinder and 2k/h for a sphere.

Example: k = 0.05 W/m K, h = 5 W/m2K: rcr = 0.01 m = 1 cm. A 5 mm wire covered up to 1 cm loses more heat than a bare one.

Fins (A4)

A fin is extra surface that conducts heat out from a wall and convects it to the air. Its temperature falls along its length, governed by d2θ/dx2 = m2θ where θ = T − T∞ and m = √(hp/kAc). The larger mL, the more the tip cools down and the less it helps.

Qfin = √(hpkAc) θb tanh(mL), ηfin = tanh(mL)/(mL)

SymbolMeaningUnit
pperimeter of the fin cross-sectionm
Accross-sectional aream2
mfin parameter √(hp/kAc)1/m
θbTbase − T∞K
ηefficiency Q/Qmax–
εeffectiveness Qfin/Qno fin–

Example: steel rod D = 2 cm, k = 50, h = 64: m = √(4 × 64/(50 × 0.02)) = 16 m−1; L = 0.25 m gives mL = 4, tanh 4 ≈ 1: it behaves as an infinitely long fin, Q = 25.1 W for θb = 100 °C.

Transient conduction (A5)

When a body is suddenly put in a hotter or colder fluid, its temperature changes with time. If its inside conducts much better than the surface convects (Bi = hLc/k < 0.1), the whole body has one temperature that approaches the fluid temperature exponentially. Otherwise use the one-term (Heisler) solution or, for a very thick body, the semi-infinite erf solution.

(T − T∞)/(Ti − T∞) = e−bt, b = hAs/(ρVcp)

SymbolMeaningUnit
BiBiot number hLc/k (inside resistance / surface resistance)–
Fo, τFourier number αt/Lc2 (dimensionless time)–
Lccharacteristic length V/Asm
binverse time constant1/s
λ1, A1one-term coefficients from tables–
erferror function–

Example: a 12 cm copper ball (k = 401) in air with h = 15: Lc = D/6 = 0.02 m, Bi = 15 × 0.02/401 = 0.00075, so lumped analysis is excellent.

Boiling and condensation (A6)

Phase change absorbs or releases latent heat hfg, so h is very large. In pool boiling the heat flux depends on the excess temperature ΔTe = Ts − Tsat along the boiling curve (natural, nucleate, transition, film). In condensation vapour forms a liquid film (film-wise) or drops (drop-wise) on a cold surface; the film is a resistance.

SymbolMeaningUnit
Tsatsaturation temperature at the given pressure°C
hfglatent heat of vaporisationJ/kg
h*fghfg + 0.68cp(Tsat − Ts), corrected for liquid subcoolingJ/kg
ρl, ρvliquid, vapour densitykg/m3
μl, klliquid viscosity, conductivitykg/m s, W/m K
Ntubes in a vertical column–
CHF (critical heat flux)critical heat flux (peak of the curve)W/m2

Example: condensation rate = Q/h*fg. If a tube bank removes 163.8 kW per m and h*fg = 2468 kJ/kg, it condenses 0.0664 kg/s of steam per metre.

Convection and boundary layers (B1, B2)

At the wall the fluid is at rest and heat enters it by conduction; the flow then carries it away. Near the wall two thin layers form: the velocity boundary layer (where the speed rises from 0 to U∞) and the thermal boundary layer (where the temperature changes from Ts to T∞). h ≈ k/δt: thin layer = big h.

SymbolMeaningUnit
ReReynolds number VL/ν (inertia/viscous)–
PrPrandtl number ν/α–
NuNusselt number hL/k (dimensionless h)–
νkinematic viscosity μ/ρm2/s
δ, δtvelocity, thermal boundary-layer thicknessm
Cffriction coefficient τs/(ρV2/2)–
Tffilm temperature (Ts + T∞)/2°C

Example: air at 3 m/s over 1.2 m: Re = 3 × 1.2/1.896×10−5 = 1.9×105 (laminar), Nu = 0.664√Re Pr1/3 = 259, h = Nu k/L = 6.1 W/m2K.

Forced convection: plates, pipes and tube banks (B3, B4, B5)

For each geometry there is a correlation Nu = C RemPrn. Flat plate: laminar below Re = 5×105. Pipe: laminar below 2300, use the bulk temperature and an exit-temperature law. Tube bank: use the maximum velocity between tubes and the Zukauskas correlation.

Te = Ts − (Ts − Ti) exp(−hAs/ṁcp), Q = hAsΔTlm

Example: tubes 1.5 cm at ST = 5 cm, air 4.5 m/s: Vmax = 5 × 4.5/(5 − 1.5) = 6.43 m/s.

Natural convection (B6)

No fan: the fluid moves because heated fluid is lighter. The strength of this flow is measured by the Rayleigh number Ra = gβΔTLc3Pr/ν2, which takes the place of Re. For air β = 1/Tf in kelvin.

SymbolMeaningUnit

Example: 0.6 m square plate, 60 K hotter than air: vertical Ra = 7.65×108, Nu = 0.59Ra1/4 = 98, h = 4.6 W/m2K, Q = 99 W.

Mass transfer (B7)

A species moves from high to low concentration by diffusion, exactly as heat moves from high to low temperature. Fick’s law JA = −CDABdyA/dx is Fourier’s law with concentration for temperature and diffusivity for conductivity. Evaporation of a liquid into still air includes an extra bulk-flow effect (a log term).

SymbolMeaningUnit
Ctotal molar concentration P/(RuT)kmol/m3
yAmole fraction of A = PA/P–
DABmass diffusivity of A in Bm2/s
NA, JAmolar flux of Akmol/m2s
Mmolar masskg/kmol
Ruuniversal gas constant 8.314kJ/kmol K
Sc, ShSchmidt ν/DAB, Sherwood hmL/DAB–

Example: air at 1 atm, 18.7 °C: C = 101.325/(8.314 × 291.85) = 0.0418 kmol/m3. Multiply a molar flux by M to get kg.
